new_bank_questions.title: What does the placebo contrast estimate?
new_bank_questions.body: In a randomized masked trial, 45 of 60 people assigned active treatment improve, compared with 30 of 60 assigned a matching placebo. Compute the two improvement proportions and the active-minus-placebo risk difference. Does the placebo group's improvement rate equal a pure expectancy effect?
new_bank_questions.answer: The proportions are 45/60=0.75 and 30/60=0.50, so the risk difference is 0.25 or 25 percentage points. The placebo improvement rate includes natural recovery, measurement fluctuation, shared care and any expectancy influence; it does not isolate expectancy.

new_bank_questions.title: Concealment and masking at different times
new_bank_questions.body: A recruiter can see the next assignment before enrolling a participant, but participants and outcome assessors are masked after enrolment. Which design protection is missing? Give one route by which it could bias the comparison, and state whether masking afterward repairs it.
new_bank_questions.answer: Allocation concealment is missing. A recruiter could preferentially enroll a sicker or healthier participant when the next assignment is known, producing baseline imbalance related to treatment. Later masking cannot undo that selection, although it can limit post-assignment behaviour and measurement biases.
